A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same score-machine theory and experiments. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison despite some inconsistent references and captions in v2.

before.justification: Sections 5–6 and Appendices C–D report original trained-model experiments, generated samples, and theory–network correlations on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10.

after.justification: V2 retains original experimental results and adds CelebA experiments, LS comparisons, and results under an additional sampling-step setting.

M1.justification: The score-machine definitions, boundary handling, time-dependent locality calibration, CNN architectures, and training objectives are retained. LS was already defined and discussed in v1; its expanded empirical evaluation does not introduce a new method.

E1.justification: V2 adds CelebA32x32 face generation and theory–network comparisons to the retained MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR10 coverage. This extends the represented image domain while retaining the same general task.

E2.justification: V1 Table 1 compares ELS with the memorizing IS baseline. V2 Tables 1–2 add the non-equivariant LS machine across all configurations, introducing a substantive alternative that directly tests the importance of equivariance.

E3.justification: V1 specifies 20-step sampling throughout. V2 adds a systematic 150-step neural-network evaluation while retaining 20 steps for analytic score machines, reporting both regimes in Tables 1–2. This materially changes the conditions underlying headline comparisons; the training budgets and correlation metric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds systematic LS-versus-ELS comparisons testing the equivariance constraint, including contrasting CelebA UNet and ResNet behavior in Section 5.4 and Figure 7. Tables 1–2 also add sampling-step sensitivity evidence. Existing padding and attention analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report median correlations and sample distributions over 100 random noise inputs per configuration. V2 introduces no new repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; additional result rows follow the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 adds LS results, CelebA outcomes, and complete 150-step results. For example, its Table 1 reports CelebA UNet correlations of 0.90 for LS versus 0.85 for ELS. Most matched 20-step results are retained, but circular-MNIST ResNet ELS correlation changes from 0.77 in v1 Table 1 to 0.73 in v2 Table 2. Higher 150-step scores are results under different conditions.

T1.justification: Definitions, assumptions, derivations, and Theorems 4.1, B.2, and B.3 remain unchanged, including their appendix proofs. Equation 5 makes the pixel argument explicit by replacing the unindexed image term with its value at x; this is a notation correction rather than revised mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract replaces unqualified training-free prediction language with an explicit locality-scale calibration condition, drops its broad 'first' claim, and includes LS and CelebA. The contribution list adds the CelebA distinction between LS and ELS. The central patch-mosaic and combinatorial-creativity claims remain.

C2.justification: New Section 5.4 substantially qualifies the role of equivariance: UNets can infer absolute position through image-wide receptive fields, explaining why LS better predicts their CelebA outputs, unlike ResNets. Appendix C.1 also acknowledges the unexplained benefit of 150-step sampling and removes the earlier MNIST-conditioning memorization rationale.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 adds an authors' code-repository link and specifies the per-step learning-rate multiplier, 0.999965, elaborating the earlier approximate 50-epoch halving description. This improves implementation disclosure without establishing a change to the underlying training schedule.

R1.justification: Six references are added, including concurrent approaches by Niedoba et al. and Wang and Vastola. The introduction describes their relationship to the proposed theory and replaces the categorical denial of prior individual-sample prediction with a more qualified comparison.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction receive focused rewrites. The boundary analysis moves within Section 5, the discussion becomes numbered, and quantitative results and sample galleries are consolidated under Appendix D. Acknowledgements and an impact statement are added; most methodological and mathematical prose remains intact.

P2.justification: Figures 1 and 5 gain CelebA examples, Figure 4 gains CelebA curves, and correlation plots are expanded and reformatted. V2 adds the architecture comparison in Figure 7, the diffusion schematic in Figure 8, and two CelebA galleries. The result table expands into two protocol-specific tables with LS columns.

improvement.justification: The LS comparisons and CelebA experiments provide a more discriminating test of the proposed mechanism, while clearer calibration qualifications and code-access information improve transparency. However, Section 5.2 mixes 20-step and 150-step results, and Figures 19–20 describe CelebA models as class-conditional despite the tables marking them unconditional. These reporting inconsistencies limit the net benefit of the useful empirical and interpretive additions.
